title: The Christian crowns turn on each other: Qashtāla and Portugal march east into Arghūn, which has Savoy and Sicily beside it. The court sees in it the fruit of its long work to split the Iberians, and an opportunity
source: Trent's account; the save of 15 March 1359 dates the war to 8 March and lists Arghūn's side

title: Sovereignty 98.4, the highest yet, and Morocco's influence 2.6. Granada can raise 6,700 men to Qashtāla's 3,900 and Portugal's 4,300; stability 31, income 62 against expenses 51

Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl, the amir's brother and his minister, marries his Aydınid bride and goes to live at her father's court in Anatolia. After Faraj, it is the second brother of the amir to leave Gharnāṭa by marriage, and the court whispers that the harem prefers the throne to have no grown brothers about it
source: Trent's account (about March 1359); the harem as the cause is the chronicle's reading, at Trent's direction

title: The New Caravanserai: at the merchants' pressing, above all the Italians who carry the better part of the realm's trade, the amir has a funduq built beside the silk market, a walled inn where wares are kept under lock and traders lodged under guard. The burghers are delighted, and the trade of Gharnāṭa and Qurṭuba flows more freely

data.choice: Build it, and let the trade flow through our gates.
data.historical: al-Funduq al-Jadīda (the Corral del Carbón) in Granada, held by the wives of the Naṣrid sultans
